intro.caption: Side B. Rule 1: say only Gerald's lines, word for word. Rule 2: when the tape stops, say the line and get their answer. Rule 3: don't tell Gerald the answer — press play. He'll know. Seat your subject, phone flat between you, face up. Play when you're both ready.

ind1.caption: 「TO YOUR SUBJECT」 Close your eyes. You're in school — ten, maybe twelve, last period, pencil in hand — doodling the same small doodle you always drew. Five, ten seconds of pencil. Not a smiley face. Not a mountain. Not a bicycle. No circles or triangles. A real thing anyone would recognize on sight. Look at it. Never say it. Play when they nod.

ind2.caption: 「TO YOUR SUBJECT」 Set the real thing in the room — actual size, between you. Now think of it as a WORD (a smiley face would be the word SMILEY). Walk its letters one at a time… and again, slower. 「TO YOU」 Ask: “Do you have it?” A nod is enough. Play when they nod.

preflight.caption: From here, only Gerald's words. Straighten up. Look like someone things happen to on purpose. Here we go.

20.caption: First one — say it like you're reading a menu: “I can feel a letter in your word. An A. There's an A… correct?” Get their answer, then play.

21.caption: There's the A — there's always an A. Next: “I see a T as well… yes?” Go.

22.caption: Two for two — don't let it change you. Softer: “Is that… an R?” Go.

23.caption: Three in a row — statistically, you're due. Last letter, barely trust it: “Now I'm not sure about this one… an S?” Go.

24.caption: That was a no — the no arrived before you did. Not the tape's fault; not the subject's. Say: “No… no, it's leaning. It's an S. There IS an S.” Like a man who has never been wrong. You've seen one.

25m.caption: A no — Gerald felt it coming, the way one feels weather. Say this as a FACT, not a question: “This thing you drew — it is NOT a living thing.” Nod = yes. Argument = no. Either way, press play.

25.caption: Agreed — not alive. Progress, the small kind. Say: “Hold out your hand. Imagine it there. Could you HOLD it in one hand?” Go.

26.caption: No R — felt through the magnetic particles, which don't lie. New approach: “Leave the letters. Let me touch the thing itself. Is it ALIVE?” Go.

27.caption: The S — we're back, and we will never speak of the A again. Now the senses: “Reach out in your mind. Can you TOUCH it?” Go.

28.caption: Also a no — Gerald knew in 1987. Letters are not your event; that's allowed. Raw impressions now: “Forget letters. Forget words. I'm getting something warmer. Is it ALIVE?” Go.

29.caption: Held it — Gerald felt the grip from in there. It's a strange life, being a tape. Say: “Squeeze it. Is it HARD?” Go.

30.caption: A no — too big for a hand. Say: “It's bigger than both of us. Tell me — do you OWN one?” Go.

31.caption: Alive — Gerald can hear it moving from here. Say: “Stand next to it in your mind. Is it SMALLER than you?” Go.

32.caption: A no — one of us is surprised. Gently: “It relates to life… it's part of a day.” Let it land. Then: “Do you have one at HOME?” Go.

33.caption: Touchable — reach further. Say: “I'm touching it with you… wait. I sense… LIFE. Is it alive?” Go.

34.caption: Alive — the impressions like you. Say: “Stand next to it. Is it BIGGER than you?” Go.

35.caption: A no — Gerald knew, the same way he knows you skipped Side A. Close now; he can feel corners. Say: “Reach for it. Can you TOUCH it?” Go.

36.caption: Wet. Gerald would stand up for this one if he could. Say: “Scales. A little bubble over its head.” Then: “You drew a FISH.” Turn the screen around.

37.caption: A no — felt in the flywheel. This next part is the whole job; say it exactly: “It's not alive — but it is FULL of life. It's where the life lives.” Watch their face. Then: “Square walls. A triangle roof. Smoke from the chimney. You drew a HOUSE.” Turn the screen around.

38.caption: Can't touch it — nobody can; that's rather the point. Say: “Of course you can't touch it. It's ninety-three million miles away — you drew it in the corner of the page with little lines coming off it. You drew the SUN.” Turn the screen around.

39.caption: Bigger, alive, and older than everyone involved. Say: “Roots down. Branches up. The leaves were one big cloud, weren't they. You drew a TREE.” Turn the screen around.

40.caption: Smaller — Gerald felt petals; he doesn't examine how. Say: “A stem. Petals in a ring. You pressed harder on the middle. You drew a FLOWER.” Turn the screen around.

41.caption: Touchable — and someone in this story has been holding its cousin the whole time. Say: “Long. Thin. A point at one end. You drew the thing you were drawing WITH. You drew a PENCIL.” Turn the screen around.

42.caption: Untouchable — called from inside a cassette, which is where Gerald lives. Say: “You drew it as a crescent — a little banana in the sky — with stars around it. You drew the MOON.” Turn the screen around.

43.caption: Hard — and cold. They didn't mention cold; they didn't have to. Say: “A stem. A bowl. A toast at the end of a long week. You drew a GLASS.” Turn the screen around. Cheers.

44.caption: Not hard — soft skin, full of air. Say: “It wants to be thrown. It spends its whole life leaving. You drew a BALL.” Turn the screen around.

45.caption: They own one — Gerald has ridden in it, in the sense that matters least. Say: “Four wheels. Windows. Parked outside a childhood house. You drew a CAR.” Turn the screen around.

46.caption: Nobody owns one — it belongs to the sky, and to a leasing company. Say: “You drew it with little windows down the side, didn't you. You drew a PLANE.” Turn the screen around.

47.caption: Smaller, warm, and profoundly uninterested in either of us. Say: “Whiskers. Pointed ears. It's ignoring you right now. You drew a CAT.” Turn the screen around.

48.caption: Not smaller — it's exactly your size. It always was. Say: “A round head. Stick arms straight out. A self-portrait, age ten. You drew a STICKMAN — you drew YOU.” Turn the screen around.

rman.caption: They argued. Good — arguments have pulses. Say: “You drew a person. Round head, stick arms straight out. That's YOU, isn't it.” Turn the screen around.

49.caption: At home, naturally — you ate off yours this evening; we'll leave it there. Say: “Four legs. A flat top. The whole family around it. You drew a TABLE.” Turn the screen around.

50.caption: Not at home — it lives on the water. Most of the good ones do. Say: “A little hull. A sail. You always drew the waves as tiny W's, didn't you. You drew a BOAT.” Turn the screen around.

51.caption: No S — and for once, a no is the best possible news. Stand up straight: “It's not letters anymore. I can FEEL this one. It's beating. You drew a HEART.” Turn the screen around. Take your time.

52.caption: Four for four. It happens — rarely, and to other people. Slowly: “You were ten years old, bored out of your mind… and you reached for the sky. You drew a STAR.” Turn the screen around. That one's yours.

finale.caption: That's the routine. Don't explain anything — you couldn't, but don't. You were adequate: Gerald's second-highest grade. No one has received the first. Press ■ to rewind for your next subject.
